messages.author: 2e9423a4b20e1401
messages.subject: Slow hierarchical logistic regression
parts:
I have a hierarchical logistic regression model with a large number of observations, and a much smaller number of groups. Here's a very simplified version:

data {
  vector[N] kk;
  vector[N] x;
  int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N];
}

parameters {
  vector[K] a;
  vector[K] b;
}

model {
  vector[N] bn;

  a ~ normal(0,100);
  b ~ normal(0,100);

  for(n in 1:N) {
    an[n] <- a[kk[n]];
    bn[n] <- b[kk[n]];
  }

  y ~ bernoulli_logit(an + ... + x .* exp(bn + ...));
}

It's vaguely similar to the model on page 56 of the Stan 1.3.0 manual. The "..." represent other terms similar to a and b that are also vectorized under the for loop. The exponential is to ensure that P(y|x) increases with x, though individual terms within the exponential may be very negative, corresponding to a flatter (but never decreasing) P(y|x) curve.

Before vectorizing this, I had it running overnight and only had ~15 warmup samples by the morning. After I vectorized it, it ran in about 20 minutes. But then in trying to tune the model, I'm finding the execution time to be very unstable, and unpredictable.
  • In my "y ~ ..." line, is it ok that y is an array, but everything else is a vector? It's not clear to me whether the two play nicely together.
  • Any suggestions for getting faster and more predictable performance?
  • Have you found profiling (gprof, etc) helpful in situations like this, or is the result too far-removed from the Stan code to be interpretable?
My last question is very different. Since N is large (about half a million), it makes some sense to speed things up by taking a subset of the data. I hate to just throw away data in a final result, so I'd have to find a way to run a few models and somehow connect them after the fact. The whole thing seems a bit flaky.

This makes me wonder about the possibility of each iteration choosing a random (or hashed, or something) subset of the N observations. This could make things go much faster, and it seems there could be connections to online algorithms. But I'm not sure if there would need to be a correction factor at runtime or after the fact to account for not using all of the data. And random number generation is only available in "generated quantities", so I'd need a hack of some sort. Any thoughts on this?

Thanks!
Chad

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow hierarchical logistic regression
parts:
The speed variations are most likely due to differences in starting point.  Chains which fail to mix or mix slowly likely started in a really bad part of the space and are having trouble escaping or adapted poorly.  One possible work around for the adaptation problem is to allow for a longer warmup.  Fixing initializations is a little hard right now (we have a bunch of things planned to fix it in the future though!).  One option is to manually specify your initializations.  If you want to run multiple chains for Rhat statistics, then you can create multiple initializations for each chain manually.

Regarding using only subsets of data, this can theoretically be done in HMC in a very nice way by using a different simulation Hamiltonian but currently Stan doesn't support this.  I'm not sure if it's really in the pipe either, but it's a good idea for handing models with really large amounts of data.

Cheers,
Marcus

> }

> individual terms within the exponential may be very negative, corresponding to a flatter (but never decreasing) P(y|x)
> curve.

Does this make more sense than constraining the terms inside
exp() to be positive?

> Before vectorizing this, I had it running overnight and only had ~15 warmup samples by the morning. After I vectorized
> it, it ran in about 20 minutes. But then in trying to tune the model, I'm finding the execution time to be very
> unstable, and unpredictable.

What are you doing for initialization?

> * In my "y ~ ..." line, is it ok that y is an array, but everything else is a vector? It's not clear to me whether the
> two play nicely together.

Yes, that's fine. When we write "reals" in the manual for an
argument in a signature, it can be a scalar or any one-dimensional
structure (array, vector, or row vector). If there's more than one
array, vector or row vector, they all have to be the same size.
That's the only restriction.

> * Any suggestions for getting faster and more predictable performance?

1. Provide reasonable inits.

2. Tighter priors (unless you reall do expect the a in a ~ normal(0,100)
to range between -300 and +300 or so). You may also want to account for
covariance, as Andrew suggested.

RMHMC should be effective when there are large number of data
points and not so many (< 1000) parameters. It deals with the
geometry issues of these hierarchical models.

> * Have you found profiling (gprof, etc) helpful in situations like this, or is the result too far-removed from the
> Stan code to be interpretable?

We know where the computation goes, so profiling per se isn't too
helpful (unless we find we've coded something badly, which profiling
can find).

Instead, Michael Betancourt's written a diagnostics package that
gets more at the geometry of the posterior. What we want to see is if
there are places where lots of rejection happens (usually high curvature)
or spots in the posterior where the sampler's getting stuck, correlations
among the parameters. The biggest problem is posterior scale variation
coupled with correlation.

Some reparameterizations can help here, like the "Matt trick".
Especially in cases of little data.

> My last question is very different. Since N is large (about half a million), it makes some sense to speed things up by
> taking a subset of the data. I hate to just throw away data in a final result, so I'd have to find a way to run a few
> models and somehow connect them after the fact. The whole thing seems a bit flaky.

We've thought about that even in just a simple linear regression case,
but there's the issue of how to scale the priors and then how to combine them.
We'd love to hear other thoughts on this.

Over the next year, we're hoping to get stochastic variational inference
working, which will only deal with part of the data at a time (providing
essentially a subgradient with expecation equal to full gradient). We're
working directly with the authors of this paper:

Stochastic Variational Inference
Matthew D. Hoffman, David M. Blei, Chong Wang, John Paisley;
JMLR 2013.
http://jmlr.org/papers/v14/hoffman13a.html

Matt's the one who developed the NUTS sampler and also explored
reparameterizations.

> This makes me wonder about the possibility of each iteration choosing a random (or hashed, or something) subset of the N
> observations. This could make things go much faster, and it seems there could be connections to online algorithms. But
> I'm not sure if there would need to be a correction factor at runtime or after the fact to account for not using all of
> the data. And random number generation is only available in "generated quantities", so I'd need a hack of some sort. Any
> thoughts on this?

Yes! See the above. I don't know if we'll figure it out for MCMC,
but we do hope to get it working for variational inference.

- Bob

PS: Did you try Passage (or another Gibbs sampler) on this model?

parts: > Ahh, this makes sense. So maybe start with a point estimate, and feed that in for the initialization value. Since Stan already computes all the gradients, it would be great to see a future version allowing something like conjugate gradient, and reporting that value before using it for initialization.
You have to be careful -- the mode isn't always a good starting point, especially in higher dimensions. But we have more sophisticated adaptation/warmup schemes in mind.
> Cool! Except when I'm writing a paper, "That's already been done" is always the best response. Do you have any citations for similar work?

http://www.mcmchandbook.net/HandbookChapter5.pdf, under "Splittings".

Trying to engineer a "stochastic" splitting is tricky because of the fact that we're doing MCMC so no matter what happens you need to loop through all of the data to have some guarantee of mixing.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow hierarchical logistic regression
parts:
On 8/23/13 7:17 PM, Chad Scherrer wrote:
> Bob,
>
> > It's vaguely similar to the model on page 56 of the Stan 1.3.0 manual. The "..." represent other terms similar to
> a and
> > b that are also vectorized under the for loop. The exponential is to ensure that P(y|x) increases with x, though
> > individual terms within the exponential may be very negative, corresponding to a flatter (but never decreasing)
> P(y|x)
> > curve.
>
> Does this make more sense than constraining the terms inside
> exp() to be positive?
>
>
> If each term is positive, that means each is only allowed to increase the slope. In the exponential approach, any term
> can increase or decrease the slope, but the slope is guaranteed to remain positive. This seemed nicer to me, though I
> may go back at some point to every term being positive, at least for comparison.

Right -- you get a bound of 0 if everything's positive.
The geometry's different for the parameters, which is why
I was suggesting it might help with speed if it made sense
that each parameter was constrained to be positive. It would
essentially do the same thing as

exp(x1) + ... + exp(xN)

through the transforms.

We don't (at least yet) have any way of putting constraints
on sets of parameters other than as part of simplexes or
covariance/correlation matrices, etc..

> > Before vectorizing this, I had it running overnight and only had ~15 warmup samples by the morning. After I
> vectorized
> > it, it ran in about 20 minutes. But then in trying to tune the model, I'm finding the execution time to be very
> > unstable, and unpredictable.
>
> What are you doing for initialization?
>
>
> Laissez-faire. Marcus suggested this could be part of the problem, so I'll look into a sensible way of doing this.

You can look at the trace plots and see what's going on.

The other alternative is to start with inits=0, which can
help, but doesn't satisfy the desire for diffuse initializations
to diagnose multimodality and other convergence difficulties.

> > * In my "y ~ ..." line, is it ok that y is an array, but everything else is a vector? It's not clear to me
> whether the
> > two play nicely together.
>
> Yes, that's fine. When we write "reals" in the manual for an
> argument in a signature, it can be a scalar or any one-dimensional
> structure (array, vector, or row vector). If there's more than one
> array, vector or row vector, they all have to be the same size.
> That's the only restriction.
>
>
> Ok, great.
>
> > * Any suggestions for getting faster and more predictable performance?
>
> 1. Provide reasonable inits.
>
> 2. Tighter priors (unless you reall do expect the a in a ~ normal(0,100)
> to range between -300 and +300 or so). You may also want to account for
> covariance, as Andrew suggested.
>
>
> Oh, that's interesting. So you think a more constrained model ought to give better computational performance?

There's always a scale implied in a normal prior and it helps
to use a realistic one for the data. It can speedup convergence
and sampling. Of course, with enough data, it's not going to make
much of a difference.

> Instead, Michael Betancourt's written a diagnostics package that
> gets more at the geometry of the posterior. What we want to see is if
> there are places where lots of rejection happens (usually high curvature)
> or spots in the posterior where the sampler's getting stuck, correlations
> among the parameters. The biggest problem is posterior scale variation
> coupled with correlation.
>
>
> Oh, nice. Is this stan-dev/visual-diagnostics?

Yes, but I have no idea how well it's documented or how complete
it is.

> Some reparameterizations can help here, like the "Matt trick".
> Especially in cases of little data.
>
>
> Not familiar with this - do you have a link?

The reparameterizations section of our manual. Roberts and crew have
also written about the centering half of the standardization:

http://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.3797.pdf

> > My last question is very different. Since N is large (about half a million), it makes some sense to speed things
> up by
> > taking a subset of the data. I hate to just throw away data in a final result, so I'd have to find a way to run a
> few
> > models and somehow connect them after the fact. The whole thing seems a bit flaky.
>
> We've thought about that even in just a simple linear regression case,
> but there's the issue of how to scale the priors and then how to combine them.
> We'd love to hear other thoughts on this.
>
> Over the next year, we're hoping to get stochastic variational inference
> working, which will only deal with part of the data at a time (providing
> essentially a subgradient with expecation equal to full gradient). We're
> working directly with the authors of this paper:
>
> Stochastic Variational Inference
> Matthew D. Hoffman, David M. Blei, Chong Wang, John Paisley;
> JMLR 2013.
> http://jmlr.org/papers/v14/hoffman13a.html <http://jmlr.org/papers/v14/hoffman13a.html>

>
> Matt's the one who developed the NUTS sampler and also explored
> reparameterizations.
>
>
> Wow! Variance inference would be really exciting.

We're psyched. I should've mentioned the other piece of the puzzle is
the general approximation for non-conjugate models:

http://arxiv.org/abs/1209.4360

>
> > This makes me wonder about the possibility of each iteration choosing a random (or hashed, or something) subset
> of the N
> > observations. This could make things go much faster, and it seems there could be connections to online
> algorithms. But
> > I'm not sure if there would need to be a correction factor at runtime or after the fact to account for not using
> all of
> > the data. And random number generation is only available in "generated quantities", so I'd need a hack of some
> sort. Any
> > thoughts on this?
>
> Yes! See the above. I don't know if we'll figure it out for MCMC,
> but we do hope to get it working for variational inference.
>
>
> PS: Did you try Passage (or another Gibbs sampler) on this model?
>
>
> Nope. We're using R pretty heavily, and Passage is Haskell-centric. Plus, it currently hard-codes the data in the C
> code, which doesn't work well for larger data.

One of the reasons we went with C++ is the ease of integration
with R, Python, etc. But you should be able to write a lightweight
wrapper around Passage to call it from R, but it's going to assume
other people have it installed. We still need a C++ compiler at run
time, which is the biggest hassle for installing Stan for R.

- Bob

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow hierarchical logistic regression
parts: On Fri, Aug 23, 2013 at 6:59 PM, Chad Scherrer <chad.s...@gmail.com> wrote:

On Friday, August 23, 2013 12:25:56 PM UTC-7, Marcus wrote:
The speed variations are most likely due to differences in starting point.  Chains which fail to mix or mix slowly likely started in a really bad part of the space and are having trouble escaping or adapted poorly.  One possible work around for the adaptation problem is to allow for a longer warmup.  Fixing initializations is a little hard right now (we have a bunch of things planned to fix it in the future though!).  One option is to manually specify your initializations.  If you want to run multiple chains for Rhat statistics, then you can create multiple initializations for each chain manually.

Ahh, this makes sense. So maybe start with a point estimate, and feed that in for the initialization value. Since Stan already computes all the gradients, it would be great to see a future version allowing something like conjugate gradient, and reporting that value before using it for initialization.

In develop there is an implementation of the BFGS optimizer which should work pretty well.  That said, as others have pointed out I wouldn't recommend the point estimate in general however, logistic regression problems are generally convex so it should work well in this case.

Here are a couple of other options just in case:

- Use init=0 to initialize everything to a single point.
- If you only want to run one chain, take note of the random seed on one of the chains that seemed to work well and use that.
- Alternatively, generate several diffuse initializations.  Throw out the ones that have issues and manually specify from those curated random initializations.

Regarding using only subsets of data, this can theoretically be done in HMC in a very nice way by using a different simulation Hamiltonian but currently Stan doesn't support this.  I'm not sure if it's really in the pipe either, but it's a good idea for handing models with really large amounts of data.

Cool! Except when I'm writing a paper, "That's already been done" is always the best response. Do you have any citations for similar work?

Check out section 5.5 of http://arxiv.org/pdf/1206.1901.pdf which talks about using an approximate Hamiltonian.  That approximate Hamiltonian could be constructed by using a subset of the data.

Cheers,
Marcus

parts:
Thanks for all the help. I think I see what's going on now. I'm using an exponential to force the slope to be positive, but the data strongly support the slope being negative. As a result, it's pushing the expression inside the exponential more and more negative. 

Sampling was taking overnight, but I was finally able to use "optimizing" (from RStan) to see what was going on.

-Chad

On 8/27/13 2:41 PM, Chad Scherrer wrote:
> Thanks for all the help. I think I see what's going on now. I'm using an exponential to force the slope to be positive,
> but the data strongly support the slope being negative. As a result, it's pushing the expression inside the exponential
> more and more negative.
>
> Sampling was taking overnight, but I was finally able to use "optimizing" (from RStan) to see what was going on.

Cool. Thanks for reporting back. I love new use cases --- hadn't
thought of using optimization for that. It's always a cause for concern
if parameters are running off to infinity or bumping up against
constraint boundaries.

As of Stan and RStan 1.3, the optimization includes the Jacobian
adjustment for the constraints (see the manual chapter for
specifics), whereas in 2.0 we eliminate it from optimization so that
we really should fit posterior modes.

- Bob
